en: The Mahāyāna Gayāśīrṣa Sūtra, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling at the mountain-top vihāra in the city of Gayā.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were formerly long-haired brahmins and had become arhats—whose taints were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, destroyed the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge were liberated; whose minds had attained mastery and who had reached the further shore. Furthermore, he was accompanied by an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had attained perfect enlightenment, he sat in tranquil meditation and entered into samādhi. Observing the dharma-realm, he thought to himself: "I have already realized bodhi; I have already attained noble wisdom;

I have already accomplished what was to be done; I have already laid down all heavy burdens; I have already emerged from the wilderness of birth and death; I have already abandoned ignorance and obtained the light of knowledge; I have already extracted the poisoned arrow; I have already exhausted craving; I have already realized the dharma-realm; I have already struck the dharma-drum, blown the dharma-conch, and raised the dharma-banner; I have abandoned the eye of birth and death and proclaimed the eye of the Dharma; I have closed the evil paths and opened the various paths of goodness; I have abandoned that which is not a field of merit and revealed the fields of merit."
As I now carefully examine such a dharma, who is able to realize it— has realized it, or will realize it?
Is it realized by the body,
or is it realized by the mind?

If one were to realize it through the body, the body is dull and inert, devoid of sensation and thought, like grass, trees, walls, or tiles and stones. Born from the four great elements and from parents, it is a phenomenon subject to impermanence, decay, and dissolution; it can only be sustained by relying on conditions such as ointments, washing, clothing, and food.
If one realizes the mind, the mind is like a magical illusion—without marks, without form, without a place of dependence, and without anything that can be contained.

Furthermore, as for bodhi, it is established by name according to worldly convention; it has no sound, no color or shape, no substantial reality, and no characteristics; it neither comes nor goes, and it neither issues forth nor enters.
Transcending the three realms, it has no location; it cannot be seen or heard, nor can it be recollected;

it is free from the sphere of objective conditions and is not an object of conceptual proliferation; it has no point of entry and is without words or letters; it is immovable and cannot be established.

It is cut off from all paths of speech, yet one speaks of "realizing," "having realized," and "will realize"; these are merely names and false conceptualizations. They are without birth, without arising, and without intrinsic nature; they cannot be grasped, cannot be spoken of, and cannot be clung to. Within this, there is truly no one who has already attained perfect enlightenment, none who is currently attaining it, and none who will attain it.
If one can thus be without realization and without attainment, only then may one be called one who has achieved perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because bodhi is free from all marks of fluctuation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, knowing what the Buddha was thinking, spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
If awakening has such characteristics, how should sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon the mind of awakening abide?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! One should abide in accordance with the characteristic of bodhi."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of bodhi?”
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!
The characteristic of bodhi transcends the triple world alone; although it possesses names in accordance with worldly convention, it is far removed from all sounds and verbal expressions."
The assembly of bodhisattvas sets out for enlightenment, yet from the very first moment they resolve their minds upon it,
there is no place toward which they proceed. Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
sons and daughters of good family should dwell in enlightenment by remaining far removed from the mind that sets out [for it].
Mañjuśrī! If bodhisattvas are able to set out toward that which is nowhere to go, they are then proceeding upon the path to enlightenment. Mañjuśrī!

To incline toward the absence of intrinsic nature is to incline toward bodhi; to incline toward the absence of a fixed location is to incline toward bodhi; to incline toward the nature of the dharma-realm is to incline toward bodhi; to incline toward non-attachment within all phenomena is to incline toward bodhi; to incline toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) as being without differentiation is to incline toward bodhi; and to incline toward that which is like a reflection in a mirror, like a shadow in light, like the moon in water, and like a mirage in the heat is to incline toward bodhi.
At that time, there was a son of the gods named Viśuddhacandraprabha in the assembly who addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Great Being! What practices do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate?”
"In dependence upon what place does one cultivate it? Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied, "O Devaputra!"
"All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the practice of great compassion by relying on the sphere of all sentient beings.
The Devaputra Viśuddhacandra then asked:
"From what kind of mind does a Bodhisattva’s great compassion arise?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: “The great compassion of a bodhisattva arises based on a mind free from flattery and deception.
He asked again:
"Upon what does a mind free from flattery and deception arise? He replied,
"A mind free from flattery and deception arises based on a mind of equality toward all sentient beings."
He asked again:
"Upon what does the mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings depend for its arising? He replied:
"It arises from the mind that takes as its basis the dharma-nature of the bases [āyatana], which is neither one nor different.
He asked again:
"From what does the mind that takes as its basis the dharma-nature of the bases, which is neither one nor different, arise?"
He replied, "It arises based on deep faith.
He asked again:
"Upon what does deep faith rely for its arising?
He replied: "It arises based upon the bodhicitta."
He asked again:
"Upon what does the bodhicitta arise? He replied:
"It arises based on the six pāramitās.
He asked again:
"On what do the six pāramitās arise?"
He replied, “It arises based on the wisdom of skillful means.
He asked again:
"Upon what do skillful means and wisdom depend for their arising? He replied:
"They arise depending upon heedfulness."
He asked again:
"Upon what does heedfulness depend? He replied:
"It arises based on the three kinds of pure conduct.
He asked again:
"On what do the three kinds of pure conduct depend for their arising?"
He replied, "It arises from the ten paths of wholesome action.
He asked again:
"Upon what do the ten paths of wholesome action depend for their arising?
He replied, "They arise depending upon the observance of pure precepts."
He asked again:
"Upon what does the upholding of pure precepts arise? He replied:
"It arises based on correct reflection.
He asked again:
"Upon what does correct reflection depend for its arising?"
He replied: "It arises based on the observation of the mind.
He asked again:
"Observe from what the mind arises?
He replied, "It arises from mindfulness that does not forget."
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhacandraprabha again asked Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: "Great Being!
How many kinds of bodhicitta do the Bodhisattvas generate that lead to accomplishment in both cause and fruit?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: “O Son of Heaven!
There are four kinds of bodhicitta generated by bodhisattvas, which bring about accomplishment in both cause and fruit.”

What are the four? First, the initial arousal of the mind; second, the arousal of the mind during the stage of practice through understanding; third, the arousal of the mind of non-retrogression; and fourth, the arousal of the mind of the stage of being born only once more before reaching buddhahood.

One should know that the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment is the cause for the stage of practice through understanding; the arousal of the mind in the stage of practice through understanding is the cause for the stage of non-retrogression; the arousal of the mind in the stage of non-retrogression is the cause for the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood; and the arousal of the mind in the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood is the cause for omniscience.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

You should know that the initial arousal of the mind is like sowing seeds in a field; the arousal of the mind during the stage of practice through understanding is like a sprout gradually growing; the arousal of the mind of non-retrogression is like branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits being produced in succession; and the arousal of the mind of the single-birth-to-Buddhahood is like the ripening of the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the mind is like a cartwright first gathering the materials; the second arousal of the mind is like having obtained the materials and treating each one individually for purification; the third arousal of the mind is like that craftsman completing the construction of the cart; the fourth arousal of the mind is like using that cart to draw heavy loads over great distances."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first production of the thought of enlightenment is like the crescent moon on the first day; the second production of the thought is like the moon from the fifth night to the seventh night; the third production of the thought is like the moon on the tenth night; and the fourth production of the thought is like the moon on the fourteenth night."
It should be known that all the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like the bright moon on the fifteenth night, when all its radiance and color are perfectly complete.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the mind transcends the stage of the śrāvaka; the second arousal of the mind transcends the stage of the pratyekabuddha; the third arousal of the mind transcends the stage of indetermination; and the fourth arousal of the mind dwells in the stage of certainty.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first production of the thought of enlightenment is like a person first learning the alphabet; the second production of the thought is like that student gradually understanding and analyzing it; the third production of the thought is like one who has studied for a long time and is skilled in calculation; the fourth production of the thought is like one whose study is matured and who thoroughly masters all treatises."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A Bodhisattva at the first production of the thought of enlightenment abides in the cause; a Bodhisattva at the second production of the thought of enlightenment abides in wisdom; a Bodhisattva at the third production of the thought of enlightenment abides in abandonment; and a Bodhisattva at the fourth production of the thought of enlightenment abides in the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised of causes; the second production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised of wisdom; the third production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised of abandonment; and the fourth production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised of the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the mind arises from causes; the second arousal of the mind arises from wisdom; the third arousal of the mind arises from abandonment; and the fourth arousal of the mind arises from the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first resolve is the section on the differentiation of causes; the second resolve is the section on the differentiation of wisdom; the third resolve is the section on the differentiation of abandonment; and the fourth resolve is the section on the differentiation of the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the bodhicitta is like gathering various medicinal herbs; the second arousal of the bodhicitta is like discerning the natures of those medicines; the third arousal of the bodhicitta is like compounding medicine according to the illness; and the fourth arousal of the bodhicitta is like taking the medicine to achieve recovery."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the mind is to be born into the family of the Dharma King; the second arousal of the mind is to study the Dharma of the Dharma King; the third arousal of the mind is to study until one attains understanding and realization; the fourth arousal of the mind is to study until one attains mastery."
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Adhimuktaprabha who addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Great Being! What is the swift path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by traveling which path the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: “O Devaputra!
There are two kinds of swift paths for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by practicing these paths, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the two? First is the path of skillful means (upāya-mārga), and second is the path of wisdom (prajñā-mārga).
The path of skillful means encompasses all wholesome dharmas; the path of wisdom is the thorough understanding and discernment [of them].
The path of skillful means does not abandon sentient beings, while the path of prajñā is able to relinquish all dharmas;
the path of skillful means knows the conjunction of dharmas, while the path of prajñā knows their non-conjunction;
the path of skillful means can act as causes and conditions, while the path of prajñā can reach quiescent extinction.

The path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*) is able to know the distinct characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*), while the path of wisdom (*prajñā-mārga*) is able to know the principle of the non-differentiation of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The path of skillful means is able to fully adorn the buddha-fields, while the path of wisdom is able to know that all buddha-fields are equal.

The path of skillful means is able to know that the faculties and practices of sentient beings are diverse, while the path of wisdom is able to know that faculties and practices are empty and non-existent.
"The path of skillful means causes all bodhisattvas to proceed to the site of enlightenment; the path of prajñā enables bodhisattvas to attain non-awakening. O Devaputra!"
Furthermore, there are two kinds of swift paths for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these two? First, the path of equipment (sambhāramārga); second, the path of discernment (nirvedhabhāgīyamārga).
The path of accumulation refers to the five perfections, such as generosity; the path of decisive resolution refers to the perfection of wisdom.
This same explanation applies to the path with attachment and the path without attachment, as well as the path with outflows and the path without outflows.
“Furthermore, there are two kinds of swift paths. What are the two?
First, the path with measure; second, the immeasurable path.”
The path with measure refers to the state of existence; the immeasurable path refers to the state of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of swift paths:
namely, the path of wisdom and the path of abandonment.
"The path of wisdom refers to the stages from the first bhūmi to the seventh bhūmi; the path of abandonment refers to the stages from the eighth bhūmi to the tenth bhūmi.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Vīryabhāvanājñānaśraddha who addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Mahāsattva!"
"What is the meaning known by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?
What is the wisdom cultivated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“Good son! Meaning is not a composite; wisdom is a composite.
The Bodhisattva Vigorous Cultivation of Wisdom and Faith said:
“O Mahāsattva! For what reason is meaning not a synthesis, while wisdom is a synthesis?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:

“Good son! Meaning is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); that which is unconditioned is not meaning. Within that which is not meaning, there is no dharma whatsoever—neither in combination nor in non-combination.”
Meaning is without change and without substantiality; it is neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned—all is taught in this way.
Good son! Wisdom is called the Path; the Path and the mind are in union, not in non-union.
"Furthermore, good son! Wisdom is only that which is in conjunction; it is not that which is not in conjunction.
The Bodhisattva Courageously Cultivating Wisdom and Faith said:
“Great Being! For what reason is wisdom only a state of conjunction and not a state of non-conjunction?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:

“Good son! Wisdom is well able to observe the aggregates, bases, and elements; it is well able to observe the law of dependent origination; and it is well able to observe what is possible and what is impossible. For this reason, it is merely a conjunction and not a non-conjunction.”
"Furthermore, good son, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten?

First is the wisdom of causes; second, the wisdom of results; third, the wisdom of meaning; fourth, the wisdom of skillful means; fifth, the wisdom of *prajñā*; sixth, the wisdom of integration; seventh, the wisdom of the *pāramitās*; eighth, the wisdom of great compassion; ninth, the wisdom of teaching and transforming sentient beings; and tenth, the wisdom of non-attachment toward all phenomena.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of undertakings. What are the ten?
First is the undertaking of the body, for the sake of purifying the bodily karma of all sentient beings.
Second is the arousal through speech, for the sake of purifying the verbal karma of all sentient beings;
third is the arousal through mind, for the sake of purifying the mental karma of all sentient beings;
fourth is the internal arousal, because of having no grasping or attachment toward any sentient beings.
Fifth is the arousal of the external, because of practicing impartial conduct toward all sentient beings;
sixth is the arousal of wisdom, because of cultivating all Buddha-wisdom;
seventh is the arousal of the buddha-fields, because of manifesting the meritorious adornments of all buddha-lands.
Eighth, the arousal [of the mind] through the transformation of sentient beings, because of knowing the medicines for the diseases of all afflictions;
ninth, the arousal of true reality, because it can accomplish the stage of certainty (*niyāma*);
tenth, the arousal of the fulfillment of unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*), because the mind has no attachment toward anything within the three realms.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of initiations of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices.

What are these ten? First, the practice of the pāramitās; second, the practice of gathering beings; third, the practice of prajñā; fourth, the practice of skillful means; fifth, the practice of great compassion; sixth, the practice of seeking the provisions for wisdom; seventh, the practice of seeking the provisions for knowledge; eighth, the practice of pure faith; ninth, the practice of entering into the truths; and tenth, the practice of not discriminating between objects of attachment and aversion.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of inexhaustible contemplations. What are these ten? First, the inexhaustible contemplation of the body;

second, the inexhaustible contemplation of phenomena; third, the inexhaustible contemplation of the Dharma; fourth, the inexhaustible contemplation of affection; fifth, the inexhaustible contemplation of views; sixth, the inexhaustible contemplation of provisions; seventh, the inexhaustible contemplation of grasping; eighth, the inexhaustible contemplation of non-attachment; ninth, the inexhaustible contemplation of correspondence; and tenth, the inexhaustible contemplation of the self-nature of consciousness at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of inexhaustible contemplations of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices for subduing. What are the ten?
First is the practice of subduing stinginess and envy, because they relinquish and give as extensively as rain.
Second, the practice of subduing the violation of precepts,
because the three karmas are pure;
third, the practice of subduing anger, because one cultivates a mind of loving-kindness.
Fourth, the practice of subduing indolence, because one seeks the Dharma without weariness;
fifth, the practice of subduing unwholesome conduct, because one attains meditative concentration, liberation, and supernormal powers;
sixth, the practice of subduing ignorance, because one generates the provisions for definitive, skillful wisdom.
Seventh, the practice of subduing all afflictions, because it brings to perfection the provisions for omniscience;
eighth, the practice of subduing perversions, because it gives rise to the path of provisions that is true and non-perverted;
ninth, the practice of subduing lack of mastery, because one attains mastery over both the opportune and the inopportune times.
Tenth is the practice of subduing attachment to the self, because one observes that all phenomena are without self.
Son of good family!
These are called the ten kinds of practices for subduing by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are ten stages of tranquility for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
First is the stage of tranquility of body, because of being far removed from the three types of unwholesome bodily actions;
second is the stage of tranquility of speech, because of purifying the four types of vocal actions;
third is the stage of tranquility of mind, because of forever abandoning the three types of evil mental conduct.
Fourth is the stage of internal tranquility, because of non-attachment to one's own self;
fifth is the stage of external tranquility, because of non-attachment to all phenomena;
sixth is the stage of tranquility through the accumulation of wisdom, because of non-attachment to the path being traversed.
Seventh is the stage of tranquility that is not self-exalting, because it observes the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom;
eighth is the stage of tranquility of ultimate-limit supernormal powers, because it gives birth to the *prajñāpāramitā*;
ninth is the stage of tranquility that extinguishes conceptual proliferation, because it does not deceive any sentient beings.
Tenth, not being attached to the state of tranquility of body and mind, because of teaching and transforming sentient beings through great compassion. Good son!
These are called the ten stages of tranquility of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice according to reality can attain bodhi; those who do not practice according to reality cannot attain it."
One who practices according to reality acts exactly as they have spoken;
one who does not practice according to reality possesses only words, being unable to have faith and acceptance, nor able to cultivate.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are two kinds of practice of reality for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these two?
First, the practice of reality as it is regarding the Path; second, the practice of reality as it is regarding cessation.
"Good son, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further have two kinds of practice of reality as it is."
What are these two?
First, the practice of self-discipline according to reality; second, the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings according to reality. "Good son!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of practice according to reality. What are these two?
First, the practice according to reality of wisdom with effort; second, the practice according to reality of wisdom without effort.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice of suchness for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these two?

First, the practice of skillfully establishing the stages according to their true nature; second, the practice of skillfully observing the non-differentiation of the stages according to their true nature. "Good son!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have two kinds of practice of suchness. What are the two?
First, the practice of suchness that skillfully distances oneself from the faults of the stages; second, the practice of suchness that skillfully perfects the merits of the stages.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice according to reality for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these two?

First, skillfully teaching the practice of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as they truly are; second, skillfully teaching the non-retrogressive dharma of the bodhi of all buddhas as it truly is.
“Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such immeasurable and boundless dharmas of true practice as these.

If one can practice in this manner according to reality, you should know that such a person will before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate and study them.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī!"
"Speak these words quickly!

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Vīryabhāvanājñānaśraddhā Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Candraprabhatejas Devaputra, Niyataraśmi Devaputra, and all others in the assembly—including gods, humans, asuras, and the rest of the world—were filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Summit of Mount Gayā (Mahāyāna-gayāśīrṣa-sūtra)
